title: John of Damascus
hookLine: a monk and father of the Eastern church who defended icons

lines: A HAMMER ON A PAINTED FACE.
A MONK PICKS UP HIS PEN.
cards: A ladder leans against a church wall. A man climbs it with a hammer and starts knocking a painted face of Christ off the plaster.
Scenes like this are remembered from the fight in the Eastern empire over icons, the painted images of Christ, Mary and the saints; you met it in year three.
One side said these pictures break the commandment and have to go. Far from the capital, a monk picked up his pen. Tradition says he had once served in the government at Damascus.
His name was John. He wrote that icons were not only allowed. They told the truth about what God had done.

teach.b: John starts by taking the objection seriously. The commandment in Exodus is real: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." He doesn't wave it away; he asks why it was given.
In the old days, he says, God had no body and no face, so no one could picture the invisible. Then God's Son took on a human face. Paul calls Christ "the image of the invisible God."
The first letter of John talks about what "we have seen with our eyes" and "our hands have handled." So, says John of Damascus, I'm not painting the invisible God. I'm painting the one people saw.
Then the daring move behind today's line. The iconoclasts thought matter was too low to carry anything holy.

teach.h: THE MAKER OF MATTER BECAME MATTER.
teach.b: John answers, in words close to these: I don't worship matter, I worship the maker of matter, who became matter for my sake, and through matter worked my salvation.
Wood, paint, bread, water, a human body: God uses all of it. So matter is not evil. Finally, he draws a line.

teach.h: WORSHIP FOR GOD, HONOR FOR IMAGES.
teach.b: An icon receives honor, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love, and the honor passes through to the person shown. Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor images this way.
Some Protestant churches keep their walls plain, reading the commandment as a reason to leave images out of worship; others use art but don't venerate it. This path ranks none of them.

how: Orthodox Christians pray before icons at home and in church, kissing them and lighting candles before them; Catholics honor statues and images in a similar way, while some Protestant churches keep worship spaces plain.

o: a monk who defended icons in the fight over images
a desert hermit who painted the first icon of Christ
an emperor who ordered icons taken from churches

games.q: John of Damascus — tap the pairs.
p: the image of the invisible God

s: John of Damascus says the commandment against images was never real
he takes it seriously and asks why it was given: no one could picture the invisible God.
John says Christians worship the wood and paint of icons
he says worship belongs to God alone; an icon receives honor that passes to the one shown.
Paul calls Christ the image of the invisible God
"the image of the invisible God," in the letter to the Colossians.

games.q: you're John. the iconoclasts say pictures of Christ break the commandment against graven images. how do you answer?
o: the invisible God became visible in Christ, so we picture the one people saw.
pictures are fine because everyone likes them.
games.why: John grounds icons in the incarnation: God's Son became human, so the one people saw with their eyes can be painted.

practice: Set an icon in front of you, on paper or a screen, or a photo of a face you love if you have none.
Look at the eyes first, then the hands, then the color, the gold or the plain background, the way you'd look at someone across a table, without analyzing. If you pray, let the looking become prayer.

wordCard.voice: John of Damascus. A monk who defended icons: because God's Son became human, the one people saw can be pictured, and the honor passes to him.

orig.note: Greek: image. Colossians 1:15 calls Christ the eikon of the invisible God; our word icon comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: matter is not evil. Wood, paint and bread can carry something holy. See you tomorrow.
